description: We are La Candona, an innovative team from Guatemala passionate about technology, science, AI, and space exploration. Our project, MARS SURVIVAL, aims to create an interactive 3D platform using real NASA data to explore Mars, plan routes, and simulate astronaut survival. We welcome creative teammates skilled in programming, AI, astronomy, GIS, 3D modeling, and UI/UX. Join us to innovate, collaborate, and proudly represent Guatemala at NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026! 🚀
summary: RedReturn is a web-based Mars excursion planner built around one question: can this crew reach a science target, survive what might go wrong, and return to base with margin? You pick a base and a target anywhere on Mars. RedReturn loads real NASA MGS MOLA elevation data for that area and plans four terrain-aware routes, shown on a relief map and in 3D. For each route it calculates oxygen, energy, water, radiation, daylight and return margin. A Monte Carlo Risk Lab stress-tests the plan, and an Emergency simulator breaks it on purpose so the crew can choose to continue, adapt or abort. Context comes from NASA space-weather alerts, Mars24 solar time and rover images, and a field card with a visor mode carries the plan into the field. It addresses the challenge by layering data from several NASA missions into an interactive route map built around crew safety. Every value is labelled as measured, calculated, assumed or simulated, and no route is ever called "safe".
details:
RedReturn: plan a Marswalk on real NASA terrain, and make it back.

What it does and how it works
The first people to walk on Mars will have no GPS, no rescue team and no second chance. Every excursion is a trade between how far the crew goes and how sure they are of getting back. RedReturn is a web-based mission planner built around one question: can this crew reach this science target, survive what might go wrong, and return to base with margin?

The crew picks a base and a target anywhere on Mars, on a close-up NASA Mars Trek map or a 3D globe. The backend loads real NASA MGS MOLA elevation data for that area. Jezero and Gale are built in; any other region is downloaded on demand, fetching only the bytes it needs from the global MOLA mosaic. Using this terrain, RedReturn plans four routes with different goals: shortest, terrain-aware, resource-conservative and science-prioritised. The terrain-aware and resource-conservative routes use A* search with a hard slope limit. It then:

  • shows them on a relief map and a navigable 3D terrain mesh, with steep slopes highlighted; computes oxygen, water, energy, radiation dose, daylight and return margin for each route;stress-tests the plan in the Risk Lab: a seeded Monte Carlo simulation (thousands of what-ifs) with P10/P50/P90 margins, the dominant failure mode, and which assumption matters most; breaks the plan on purpose in the Emergency simulator (battery loss, slow rover, oxygen leak, delays) and compares continuing, skipping the science stop, or aborting and returning; adds context: Mars season and local solar time computed with NASA GISS's Mars24 algorithm, live NASA DONKI space-weather alerts, and the latest Perseverance/Curiosity raw images near the base; produces a leg-by-leg field card (bearing, distance, climb, arrival time, oxygen left), a high-contrast visor mode, and PDF, JSON and GeoJSON reports.

Trips longer than about 150–180 km switch to a clearly labelled long-range overview route that estimates travel time, sols and supplies.

Benefits and intended impact
RedReturn turns open NASA data into the decision astronauts will actually face: go, adapt, or come home. For mission planners it is a fast, explainable "what-if" tool. For students and the public it is a hands-on way to learn about EVA planning, uncertainty and risk. A guided tour, a glossary and plain-language next steps make it understandable to anyone, and it works on phones, tablets and desktops.

How it is creative
Most route maps draw a path and stop there. RedReturn goes further. It asks how the plan fails, explains why with an assistant (ARES) that answers only from its own calculations, and ends in a field-ready visor. Every mission is saved in a shareable link.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty. Every value is labelled as measured, calculated, assumed or simulated. Map imagery is never used as elevation, and missing data is never filled in. The 463 m grid cannot see boulders, and the app says so next to every route. Monte Carlo output is not presented as a survival probability. No route is ever called "safe": it is a research and education prototype, not operational guidance.
  • Reproducibility. The calculations are deterministic and seeded, and reports carry SHA-256 hashes. 16 independent recomputation checks confirm the demo results.
  • Reliability and accessibility. Typed error messages with retry buttons, and a labelled offline snapshot mode. Accessibility is checked with axe at 375, 768 and 1280 px.
  • Testing. 80 frontend and 90 backend unit tests pass, plus 37 end-to-end browser tests and 38 live API checks.

Tools and languages

  • Frontend: TypeScript, React 19 and Next.js 15 (static export), React Three Fiber and Three.js for 3D, Recharts, Zustand and Tailwind CSS.
  • Backend: Python 3.12 with FastAPI and NumPy.
  • Testing: Vitest, Pytest, and Playwright with axe-core.
  • Hosting: Netlify for the website (redreturngt.us) and Google Cloud Run for the API (Docker).
  • NASA data: MGS MOLA DEM (USGS/NASA), NASA Mars Trek (MOLA, Viking, THEMIS, TES), the Mars24 algorithm, CCMC DONKI, Mars rover raw images and MSL RAD dose. AI coding assistants (Codex and Claude) helped with development. Every number comes from deterministic, tested code.
